claims.text: The Q235 steel is initially in the as-received, pre-exposure condition with a standard mill-finished surface.
Corrosion degradation or temporary protection of Q235 steel in an aggressive salt environment is governed by the rate and quality of oxide-scale formation.
Exposure at 700–900 °C produces faster oxidation kinetics than exposure at room temperature.
Exposure at 700–900 °C promotes a relatively dense and adherent oxide scale on Q235 steel.
The high-temperature oxide scale is predominantly magnetite (Fe3O4).
A dense, adherent high-temperature oxide scale transiently slows further corrosive attack or mass loss.
Room-temperature exposure produces slower oxidation kinetics than exposure at 700–900 °C.
Slower room-temperature oxidation produces a discontinuous, porous, and poorly adherent oxide film on Q235 steel.
The room-temperature oxide film permits continued penetration of corrosive salt and faster degradation.
Holding salt type, salt amount, exposure duration, and specimen geometry constant is intended to isolate temperature as the intervention.
High-temperature specimens should have a denser and better-adhered oxide scale than room-temperature specimens.
High-temperature specimens should exhibit lower net mass gain, or a mass change interpreted as slower progressive corrosion, than room-temperature specimens.
Room-temperature specimens should exhibit more significant corrosion damage than high-temperature specimens.
High-temperature specimens might show a moderate surface-hardness increase due to scale formation relative to the baseline.
The proposed mechanism is expected to apply only when temperature is high enough, identified here as 700–900 °C, to markedly accelerate oxidation kinetics.
Below the stated high-temperature regime, oxide formation and corrosion protection may differ and the proposed mechanism may not apply.
Prior quantitative data for Q235 steel under the proposed extreme salt-exposure conditions are limited.
